title: NVIDIA Updates Rubin GPU Specs as First Production Hardware Arrives
gist: NVIDIA quietly revised Rubin's shipping specs as Vera Rubin NVL72 ramps in Q4 2026: per-GPU HBM4 bandwidth cut ~11% (22 to 19.2TB/s) and NVLink scale-up bandwidth cut 17% (3.6 to 3.0TB/s), while scale-out networking rises to 450GB/s. HGX Rubin NVL8 takes the biggest hit, losing 13% of HBM4 capacity (2.3TB to 2.0TB) and 26% of memory bandwidth, with FP4/FP8 training figures also trimmed.

insights.claim: NVIDIA's shipping Rubin GPU spec cuts HBM4 memory bandwidth from a preliminary 22TB/s to 19.2TB/s (about 11% lower), implying per-pin data rates fell from ~10.75Gbps to ~9.375Gbps across 8 HBM4 stacks.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Memory-bound AI workloads on Rubin will see less per-GPU uplift than buyers modeled from the 2025-era preliminary specs.
insights.quote: But with these revised shipping specifications, a single Rubin GPU will now provide 19.2TB/second of bandwidth, for a data rate of about 9.375Gbps/pin
insights.locator: Compared to NVIDIA’s preliminary specifications, the HBM4

insights.claim: Rubin's NVLink scale-up bandwidth per GPU is cut from 3.6TB/s to 3.0TB/s, a 600GB/s (17%) reduction, in the fabric NVIDIA uses to make many GPUs act as one.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: NVLink has been NVIDIA's key differentiation vs. merchant interconnects; a shortfall here narrows the gap in rack-scale scale-up claims.
insights.quote: That is now a flat 3.0TB/second, a 600GB/second (or 17%) reduction.
insights.locator: NVLink interconnect bandwidth is also taking a hit

insights.claim: Scale-out networking bandwidth per Rubin GPU rises from a preliminary 400GB/s to 450GB/s, the only bandwidth figure that improved versus the preliminary spec.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Large multi-rack deployments leaning on scale-out networking get more headroom than originally projected, a positive for networking attach.
insights.quote: For a single Rubin GPU, NVIDIA is offering 450GB/second of networking bandwidth, up from their preliminary specification of 400GB/second.
insights.locator: While NVLink (scale-up) bandwidth has been reduced

insights.claim: Rubin's compute and memory capacity are shipping at spec: 50 PFLOPS NVFP4 inference, 35 PFLOPS NVFP4 training and 288GB of HBM4 per GPU are unchanged, meaning NVIDIA hit its clock-speed and capacity targets.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: The shortfall is in the memory/interconnect subsystem, not the GPU die itself, so it reads as a supply-chain/IO limitation rather than a silicon miss.
insights.quote: So NVIDIA has hit its clock speed and memory-capacity targets for the GPU.
insights.locator: Beyond these changes, NVIDIA has not changed

insights.claim: NVIDIA has not explained the HBM4 bandwidth cut; ServeTheHome's working assumption is that NVIDIA and its memory partners could not deliver the targeted speeds, whether due to memory controller speeds, memory stack speeds, stack yields at the target speed, or a combination.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Points to HBM4 speed-bin yields as a binding constraint in the AI supply chain, relevant to memory suppliers' mix and pricing.
insights.quote: the immediate assumption is that NVIDIA and its memory partners cannot deliver on those specs, be it memory controller speeds, memory stack speeds, memory stack yields

themes.theme: HBM4 data-rate race vs JEDEC and AMD

insights.claim: Even after the cut, Rubin's ~9.375Gbps/pin HBM4 rate remains well above the official HBM4 specification target of 8Gbps/pin, which itself doubled bus width per stack to 2048 bits versus HBM3E.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is still demanding above-spec HBM4 bins, keeping pressure on memory makers to deliver premium high-speed parts.
insights.quote: NVIDIA’s 10.75Gbps rate was significantly higher than the original HBM4 specification, and even their newly reduced 9.375Gbps data rate is still quite a bit above.

insights.claim: AMD's MI455X runs its HBM4 stacks at only 7.6Gbps/pin, so NVIDIA's revised Rubin memory rate is still significantly higher than some other HBM4 consumers.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: The downgrade does not by itself erase Rubin's per-pin memory speed lead over AMD's MI455X.

themes.theme: Vera Rubin NVL72 rack revised in lockstep

insights.claim: Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-level GPU memory bandwidth falls from 1,580TB/s to 1,400TB/s (an 11% / 180TB/s cut) while HBM4 capacity stays at 20.7TB.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: NVIDIA's flagship rack ships with less memory bandwidth than sell-side and customer TCO models built on preliminary specs assumed.
insights.quote: cumulative GPU memory bandwidth has gone from 1,580TB/second to 1400TB/second for the rack-scale system, a net loss of 180 TB (11%)
insights.locator: For NVL72, its specifications have been revised

insights.claim: NVL72 rack NVLink scale-up bandwidth is revised from 260TB/s to 216TB/s, while rack scale-out networking rises from 28.8TB/s to 32.4TB/s (bidirectional).
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Shifts the relative value toward scale-out fabrics for very large clusters.
insights.quote: NVIDIA’s plans to offer 260TB/second of bandwidth across the rack have been revised down to 216TB/second
insights.locator: NVLink bandwidth across the system for its scale-up

insights.claim: ServeTheHome doubts an NVL72 rack can reach the AI performance originally intended given lower memory and NVLink bandwidth, though the GPU and CPU compute hardware ships at spec.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Expect real-world Rubin performance-per-rack gains to land below the headline marketing ratios versus Blackwell.
insights.quote: Whether an NVL72 rack can hit quite the same level of AI performance with less memory and NVLink bandwidth as originally intended seems doubtful
insights.locator: Past this, the rest of the figures for Vera

insights.claim: The Vera Rubin ramp is in progress in Q4 2026, with hyperscalers making some of the first NVL72 systems generally available to customers.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Rubin revenue recognition is underway; spec changes apply to all shipping volume from day one.
insights.quote: NVIDIA and its partners are in the middle of the Vera Rubin ramp-up, including hyperscalers making some of the first NVL72 systems generally available to their customers
insights.locator: As we roll into the fourth quarter

themes.theme: HGX Rubin NVL8 takes the biggest hit

insights.claim: HGX Rubin NVL8 loses 300GB (13%) of HBM4, from 2.3TB to 2.0TB, implying each GPU has only ~250GB enabled, which requires just 7 of Rubin's 8 HBM4 stacks.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Disabling an HBM stack on 8-way parts suggests NVIDIA is harvesting partially-yielding packages or rationing HBM4 supply into the lower-tier SKU.
insights.quote: However, a 2.0TB setup means each GPU needs only around 250GB of HBM4 available. That, in turn, requires only 7 of the GPU’s 8 HBM4 memory stacks.
insights.locator: NVIDIA’s preliminary figure would require each Rubin

insights.claim: NVL8 memory bandwidth falls 26% (about 46TB/s), from 176TB/s to 130TB/s, or ~16.8TB/s per GPU, the largest bandwidth reduction in the Rubin family.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Enterprise and smaller-cloud buyers of 8-way HGX boxes get a materially weaker memory subsystem than the flagship rack.
insights.quote: Rather than losing just 11% of its memory bandwidth, it is losing 26%, or about 46TB/second.
insights.locator: Consequently, NVL8 is taking the biggest memory

insights.claim: NVL8 FP4 training is cut from 280 to 270 PFLOPS and FP8 training from 140 to 130 PFLOPS, while FP4 inference stays at 400 PFLOPS and scale-out networking rises from 1.6TB/s to 1.8TB/s.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Training throughput claims on the 8-way platform are modestly lower; inference headline unchanged.
insights.quote: FP4 training performance has been reduced from 280 PFLOPS to 270, and FP8 training has similarly been dialed down from 140 PFLOPS to 130

insights.claim: The NVL8 changes apply to both HGX Rubin NVL8 (Rubin + x86 CPU) and HGX Vera Rubin NVL8 (Rubin + Vera), as well as DGX systems built on the NVL8 platform; the Vera Rubin Superchip and NVL4 are also revised.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: OEM/ODM 8-way server partners ship the reduced configuration across the board.
insights.quote: these changes affect both versions of the HGX NVL8, as well as DGX systems based on the NVL8 platform

themes.theme: Interpretation: NVIDIA trading ambition for volume

insights.claim: ServeTheHome reads the revisions as NVIDIA reining in Rubin's ambitions to bring it to market at the scale it targets, with the real performance impact workload-dependent since not all workloads are equally memory- or network-bound.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Volume and schedule were prioritized over peak specs, which supports Rubin shipment volumes even as per-unit performance softens.
insights.quote: It seems NVIDIA has had to rein in its ambitions for the Rubin GPU to bring the product to market at the scale they are aiming for

insights.claim: NVIDIA posted the revised specs quietly in September on its webpages and architecture datasheet; they were first spotted by IT Home, and NVIDIA had flagged preliminary values as subject to change.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Spec changes surfaced without a formal announcement, so monitoring datasheets can front-run narrative shifts.
insights.quote: back in September NVIDIA posted the updated specifications for its Rubin GPU and various Rubin-based products on their webpages and in NVIDIA’s architecture datasheet
insights.locator: As initially spotted by IT Home
